one_liner: C++ async RPC framework with a built-in persistent server queue; the vendor claims 3.6-54x RabbitMQ's enqueue/dequeue speed.
what_it_does: SocketPro is UDAParts' client/server communication framework on non-blocking TCP. One server port hosts many services (RPC, pub/sub, HTTP/websocket, routing), which are loaded as plugins. The persistent message queue is one of those plugins (uasyncqueue), and it exposes named queue files on the server. Clients take a CAsyncQueue handler from a CSocketPool and call Enqueue/EnqueueBatch(key, msgId, bytes), Dequeue(key, callback, timeout) (which returns messages in batches), StartQueueTrans/EndQueueTrans, FlushQueue and CloseQueue through callbacks, futures or C++20 co_await, with wire-compatible adapters for C++, .NET, Java, Python, Node.js, PHP and Go. It is not AMQP: there are no exchanges, bindings or routing keys, so replacing RabbitMQ means rewriting producers and consumers against SocketPro's own protocol and running its server.
how_it_is_fast: Requests are pipelined: a client keeps sending without waiting for replies, and both the client and server cores merge pending requests and results into full TCP packets. The vendor calls this 'inline batching', and Nagle's algorithm is disabled. Each Dequeue returns a batch of messages (16 KB by default, 32 KB in the benchmark server), and the benchmark keeps three Dequeue requests in flight so that disk reads, network transfer and client parsing overlap. On the server, enqueues under 4 KB run on the main thread to avoid a thread handoff, and EnqueueBatch commits many messages as one job. Two more factors matter. Queue writes default to oMemoryCached, which buffers them in process memory (revision 6.0.2.5), with FlushQueue pushing them to the OS cache or disk. The storage engine lives in the closed-source server core binary, so its file format and indexing cannot be inspected.
when_to_use: You already build on SocketPro RPC (C++, .NET, Java, Python or Node.js) and want a work queue served from the same server process and port, without running a separate broker.

Windows or x86-64 Linux hosts where producers stream many 200 B-1 KB messages and consumers drain in bulk, especially over higher-latency links where pipelining hides round trips. The vendor's largest gains are in this range.

Producers must not lose messages during broker or network outages. An optional client-side queue file backs up every request and replays it after reconnect, and the tutorial shows this surviving repeated server kills.
You are maintaining or re-measuring a legacy UDAParts deployment. The in-repo qperf drivers (C++, C#, Java, RabbitMQ C#) and the Kafka command lines let you rerun the comparisons.
when_not_to_use: You need AMQP, MQTT or the Kafka protocol, exchange or topic fan-out semantics, clustering or quorum queues, or ecosystem tooling such as a management UI. None of these exist, and the only way to interoperate is through SocketPro adapters.

You need license-clear or auditable code. There is no LICENSE file, the client and server cores ship only as prebuilt .dll/.so files, and the changelog mentions an 'enterprise license'. Only the adapters and plugins such as the queue come as source.

Tiny (4-32 B) messages without manual batching: the vendor's own 2017 Kafka study found Kafka about 20% faster at both writing and reading them. In that study, cross-machine dequeue of medium and large messages was roughly equal to Kafka.

You need maintained software or other platforms. The last commit was in February 2023, issues #3 and #4 (2017, 2019) have no replies, there are no GitHub releases, and binaries exist only for x86-64 Linux, Windows x86/x64 and a Windows CE client. There are none for macOS or aarch64.

You need per-message disk durability by default. Queues default to oMemoryCached, and a signal handler writes cached messages to the file on shutdown. Behavior on kill -9 or power loss is not documented.

integration.form: shared lib: prebuilt closed-source cores (usocket.dll/libusocket.so for the client, UServerCore.dll/libuservercore.so for the server) plus the uasyncqueue plugin .dll/.so. The plugin source is in include/queue/server_impl, and the C++ client adapter is compiled from include/aclientw.cpp and membuffer.cpp.
integration.dependencies: The prebuilt SocketPro core and plugin libraries, copied into /usr/lib or System32/SysWOW64. OpenSSL: the docs say 1.1.0+ and the 6.4 changelog says the cores link OpenSSL 3. libdl and pthread on Linux, and the Visual C++ 2015-2019 redistributable on Windows.
integration.min_toolchain: C++11: the dev guide says so, and the qperf Makefile uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3. The co_await samples need C++20 coroutines. Tested compiler versions are not documented beyond Visual Studio 2015-2019 and g++ via NetBeans.
integration.platforms: Windows x86/x64 and Linux x86-64 (one binary set for Debian, Ubuntu, CentOS, RHEL and openSUSE), plus a Windows CE client (armv4i/x86). No macOS or aarch64 binaries.
integration.thread_safety: The docs say the core libraries, socket pools and each pooled socket are thread-safe. The queue plugin guards each queue with a critical section and the key-to-queue map with a spin lock, and a queue may be shared by several producers and consumers at once.

gotchas: The benchmark is not like-for-like. The RabbitMQ consumer in samples/qperf/rabbitmq/Program.cs sets BasicQos prefetch=1 and acks every message manually, so it pays one round trip per message. Cross-machine RabbitMQ dequeue took 44.4 s for 200-char and 45.4 s for 1024-char messages (about 444 us per message, flat with size), which fits that bottleneck. RabbitMQ enqueue timing stops when the BasicPublish loop returns (no publisher confirms), while SocketPro's waits for every server reply.

The benchmark servers (cperf sq_server.cpp and the C# sq_server) never call FlushQueue or SetOptimistic, so the 'durable' SocketPro numbers ran at the oMemoryCached default. Call FlushQueue(key, cb, tagOptimistic::oDiskCommitted) when you need data committed to disk.

Dequeue is batch-and-repeat: your DDequeue callback must re-issue Dequeue while messageCount > 0, and throughput depends on keeping 2-3 requests in flight. The consumer must deserialize payloads with the same types and order the producer used (CUQueue), because there is no schema.

The plugin opens every queue with a hard-coded ttl of 120 hours (StartQueue(key, 120*3600)), and what expires is not documented. CloseQueue fails with QUEUE_DEQUEUING while messages are mid-dequeue, and the plugin drops all queue handles when its last client disconnects.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings replace Kafka, NATS or ZeroMQ (Redpanda, Woodpecker, FluxMQ, Zenoh, Wisp, TCPSHM), and none targets RabbitMQ-style work queues. Pick SocketPro only if you are committed to its RPC framework and want the queue inside that server. For a maintained, durable, open log use Redpanda, and for crash-recoverable broker-less C++ point-to-point messaging use MIT-licensed TCPSHM.
verified_claims_summary: The vendor's 2016 study (PDF in the repo, HTML archived in 2020) enqueued and dequeued 100,000 persistent 200/1024/10240-char messages with the RabbitMQ .NET tutorial clients (RabbitMQ version, compiler and flags not stated). On one i7-4770 running Windows 8.1, SocketPro was 3.6-26x faster (200-char dequeue 14,129 -> 544 ms). Across 1 Gbps to a 4 GB Xeon E5-2630 v2 Windows Server 2012R2 VMware broker it was 4.3-10.9x faster on enqueue and 9.8-54x on dequeue (200-char dequeue 44,400 -> 820 ms), with RabbitMQ's consumer limited to prefetch 1 and per-message acks. A separate 2017 in-repo study against Kafka 0.10.1.1 (acks=1, Ubuntu 16.04, i7-4770, 7200-rpm HDD) reported SocketPro about 20-25% faster at writing medium and large messages, but Kafka about 20% faster on unbatched 4-32 B messages.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit is 2023-02-16 (v6.4), udaparts.com no longer resolves and old issues have no replies. With no license and a closed binary core, it is a reference design, not something you can legally vendor or patch.
